source: The intense Pequod sailed on; the rolling waves and days went by; the life-buoy-coffin still lightly swung; and another ship, most miserably misnamed the Delight, was descried. As she drew nigh, all eyes were fixed upon her broad beams, called shears, which, in some whaling-ships, cross the quarter-deck at the height of eight or nine feet; serving to carry the spare, unrigged, or disabled boats.

Upon the stranger’s shears were beheld the shattered, white ribs, and some few splintered planks, of what had once been a whale-boat; but you now saw through this wreck, as plainly as you see through the peeled, half-unhinged, and bleaching skeleton of a horse.
“Look!” replied the hollow-cheeked captain from his taffrail; and with his trumpet he pointed to the wreck.

“The harpoon is not yet forged that ever will do that,” answered the other, sadly glancing upon a rounded hammock on the deck, whose gathered sides some noiseless sailors were busy in sewing together.

“Not forged!” and snatching Perth’s levelled iron from the crotch, Ahab held it out, exclaiming—“Look ye, Nantucketer; here in this hand I hold his death! Tempered in blood, and tempered by lightning are these barbs; and I swear to temper them triply in that hot place behind the fin, where the White Whale most feels his accursed life!”

“Then God keep thee, old man—see’st thou that”—pointing to the hammock—“I bury but one of five stout men, who were alive only yesterday; but were dead ere night. Only that one I bury; the rest were buried before they died; you sail upon their tomb.” Then turning to his crew—“Are ye ready there? place the plank then on the rail, and lift the body; so, then—Oh! God”—advancing towards the hammock with uplifted hands—“may the resurrection and the life——”
“Brace forward! Up helm!” cried Ahab like lightning to his men.

But the suddenly started Pequod was not quick enough to escape the sound of the splash that the corpse soon made as it struck the sea; not so quick, indeed, but that some of the flying bubbles might have sprinkled her hull with their ghostly baptism.
As Ahab now glided from the dejected Delight, the strange life-buoy hanging at the Pequod’s stern came into conspicuous relief.
“Ha! yonder! look yonder, men!” cried a foreboding voice in her wake. “In vain, oh, ye strangers, ye fly our sad burial; ye but turn us your taffrail to show us your coffin!”

modern_en.title: Chapter 131 — The Pequod Meets The Delight
paragraphs: The intense Pequod sailed on; the rolling waves and days went by; the life-buoy coffin still swung lightly; and another ship, most miserably misnamed the Delight, was sighted. As she drew near, all eyes were fixed on her broad beams, called shears, which in some whaling ships cross the quarter-deck at a height of eight or nine feet, serving to carry the spare, unrigged or disabled boats.

On the stranger's shears could be seen the shattered white ribs and a few splintered planks of what had once been a whale-boat; but you could now see through this wreck as plainly as you see through the peeled, half-unhinged, bleaching skeleton of a horse.

"Look!" the hollow-cheeked captain answered from his taffrail, and pointed his trumpet at the wreck.
"Have you killed him?"

"Not forged!" — and snatching Perth's leveled iron from the crotch, Ahab held it out, exclaiming — "Look here, Nantucketer; here in this hand I hold his death! These barbs are tempered in blood, and tempered by lightning; and I swear to temper them a third time in that hot place behind the fin, where the White Whale most feels his accursed life!"

"Then God keep you, old man — do you see that?" — pointing to the hammock — "I am burying only one of five stout men who were alive only yesterday but were dead before night. Only that one do I bury; the rest were buried before they died; you sail upon their tomb." Then, turning to his crew — "Are you ready there? Place the plank on the rail, then, and lift the body; so, then — Oh! God" — advancing toward the hammock with uplifted hands — "may the resurrection and the life —"
"Brace forward! Up helm!" cried Ahab like lightning to his men.

But the suddenly started Pequod was not quick enough to escape the sound of the splash the corpse soon made as it struck the sea; not quick enough, indeed, to keep some of the flying bubbles from perhaps sprinkling her hull with their ghostly baptism.
As Ahab now glided away from the dejected Delight, the strange life-buoy hanging at the Pequod's stern stood out in sharp relief.
"Ha! Over there! Look over there, men!" cried a foreboding voice in her wake. "In vain, oh you strangers, do you flee our sad burial; you only turn your taffrail to us to show us your coffin!"

modern_da.title: Kapitel 131 — Pequod møder Delight
paragraphs: Den intense Pequod sejlede videre; de rullende bølger og dage gik; livbøjekisten svingede stadig let; og endnu et skib, mest ulykkeligt fejlnavngivet Delight, blev set. Da hun kom nærmere, var alle øjne rettet mod hendes brede bjælker, kaldet sakse, som på nogle hvalfangerskibe krydser agterdækket i en højde af otte eller ni fod og bruges til at bære de ekstra, urigede eller ubrugelige både.

På den fremmedes sakse kunne man se de knuste hvide spanter og nogle få splintrede planker af, hvad der engang havde været en hvalbåd; men man kunne nu se lige så tydeligt igennem dette vrag, som man ser igennem en hests afskallede, halvt ud af led, blegende skelet.
»Har I set den hvide hval?«
»Se!« svarede den hulkindede kaptajn fra agterrælingen og pegede med sin trompet på vraget.
»Har I dræbt ham?«
»Den harpun, der nogensinde gør det, er endnu ikke smedet,« svarede den anden og så bedrøvet på en rund hængekøje på dækket, hvis sammenfoldede sider nogle tavse sømænd var i gang med at sy sammen.

»Ikke smedet!« — og Ahab snuppede Perths vandrette jern fra gaflen, holdt det frem og udbrød — »Se her, nantucketer; her i denne hånd holder jeg hans død! Disse modhager er hærdet i blod og hærdet af lyn; og jeg sværger at hærde dem en tredje gang på det hede sted bag finnen, hvor den hvide hval mest føler sit forbandede liv!«

»Så Gud bevare dig, gamle mand — ser du det?« — og han pegede på hængekøjen — »Jeg begraver kun én af fem stærke mænd, som var i live i går, men døde, før natten kom. Kun den ene begraver jeg; de andre blev begravet, før de døde; du sejler hen over deres grav.« Så vendte han sig mod sin besætning — »Er I klar derovre? Læg planken op på rælingen, så, og løft liget; sådan, ja — Åh! Gud« — og han gik frem mod hængekøjen med løftede hænder — »må opstandelsen og livet —«
»Brasse frem! Op med roret!« råbte Ahab som et lyn til sine mænd.

Men den pludseligt sat i gang Pequod var ikke hurtig nok til at undslippe lyden af plasket, som liget snart gav, da det ramte havet; ikke hurtig nok, ja, til at holde nogle af de flyvende bobler fra måske at stænke hendes skrog med deres spøgelsesagtige dåb.
Da Ahab nu gled væk fra den nedtrykte Delight, trådte den mærkelige livbøje, der hang ved Pequods hæk, skarpt frem.

»Ha! Derovre! Se derover, mænd!« råbte en uhyggeligt varslende stemme i hendes kølvand. »Forgæves, åh I fremmede, flygter I fra vores sørgelige begravelse; I vender kun agterrælingen mod os for at vise os jeres kiste!«
